query: Design a hypothesis for the synthesis of a CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy that overcomes the low hardness and porosity associated with casting by utilizing the synergistic effects of prolonged high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering. The hypothesis must posit that milling durations of ~6 hours induce sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement to lower the energy barrier for a specific FCC/BCC solid solution transition, while SPS at 1000°C facilitates densification without triggering excessive HCP precipitation driven by Ti. Use the principle that VEC and atomic radius mismatch govern the phase stability in this specific transition. Identify the boundary where sintering temperature exceeds the threshold for grain growth or phase decomposition, and specify a falsification experiment involving Vickers hardness testing at low loads to isolate grain boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening. Ensure the hypothesis does not rely on post-hoc optimization of the exact sintering curve but rather on the fundamental thermodynamics of the ball-milled state.

generation.hypothesis: Prolonged high-energy ball milling (~6 hours) of CoCrFeNiTi elemental powders induces sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement to lower the energy barrier for a BCC-to-FCC solid solution transition, while subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1000°C facilitates near-complete densification without triggering excessive HCP precipitation driven by Ti, provided the Valence Electron Concentration (VEC) and atomic radius mismatch (δ) are maintained within specific stability windows.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi elemental powder blend with high porosity and coarse grain structure, exhibiting low hardness typical of cast or as-mixed states.
generation.intervention: High-energy ball milling for ~6 hours followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1000°C under vacuum or inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Milling atmosphere: Argon; SPS temperature: 1000°C; SPS pressure: 50 MPa; Heating rate: 100°C/min; Dwell time: 10 min.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement to nanocrystalline scale and induced lattice strain from milling, which alters the thermodynamic stability landscape favoring the FCC phase formation over HCP, mediated by VEC and atomic size mismatch parameters.
generation.mechanism: Ball milling introduces high dislocation density and reduces grain size, lowering the activation energy for the BCC-to-FCC transition. The specific VEC of CoCrFeNiTi (calculated to be ~7.4) and atomic radius mismatch (δ ~4.5%) place the alloy in a metastable region where FCC is favored at elevated temperatures but HCP is kinetically accessible. SPS at 1000°C provides sufficient thermal energy for diffusion and densification while staying below the threshold for excessive HCP precipitation (which typically requires higher temperatures or longer dwell times for Ti-rich phases to nucleate and grow). The rapid heating and cooling of SPS suppresses the formation of brittle intermetallics and HCP phases that would otherwise degrade mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: A fully dense (relative density >98%) CoCrFeNiTi alloy with a predominantly FCC solid solution matrix, significantly enhanced Vickers hardness (>600 HV) compared to cast counterparts, and minimal HCP precipitation. The microstructure will exhibit ultrafine grains (<1 μm) and high dislocation density, contributing to strength via grain boundary strengthening and solid solution strengthening.
generation.baseline: Cast CoCrFeNiTi alloy with low hardness (~200-300 HV), high porosity (>5%), and mixed BCC/FCC/HCP phases leading to poor mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: SPS temperature must not exceed 1100°C to avoid excessive grain growth and the nucleation of Ti-rich HCP phases. Milling time must be optimized to ~6 hours; excessive milling (>10 hours) may introduce too much oxygen contamination leading to oxide precipitation, while insufficient milling (<4 hours) fails to induce the necessary lattice strain for the phase transition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold for HCP precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi under SPS conditions is not precisely defined in the literature, and the influence of trace oxygen contamination during milling on phase stability remains a variable. The predicted hardness range assumes ideal densification and may vary if residual porosity persists.
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct Vickers hardness testing on samples sintered at 1000°C with varying milling times (4h, 6h, 8h) using low loads (10g-50g) to isolate grain boundary strengthening effects. If hardness does not increase significantly with milling time up to 6h and then plateau or decrease, or if XRD analysis reveals dominant HCP peaks instead of FCC, the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, if relative density remains below 95% despite SPS at 1000°C, the densification mechanism is invalid.

3.1. Microstructure and Phase Transition

Figure 1 a shows the XRD patterns of the equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi high entropy alloy powders with different milling times. Diffraction peaks of all the pure elements can be observed in the initial blend. At the beginning of ball milling, the peak intensity of Ti, Nb, Ta, and V decrease more rapidly than W and Mo. Subsequently, two overlapping peaks near the peaks of W and Mo, characterized as body-centered cubic (BCC) solutions, are observed in the XRD pattern after 20 h. It can be hypothesized that the solid solution sequence of the elements is related to the melting point, with low-melting-point elements being dissolved more quickly than the elements with higher melting points, which has been similarly reported in the previous work [ [18] ]. In order to obtain alloy powders with homogeneous composition, the milling time is prolonged to 40 h. The equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi HEA powders after 40 h of milling had an average particle size of less than 10 μm, as shown in Figure 1 b, and the SAED pattern of them is shown in the inset of Figure 1 b. 4.1. Phase Formation

Although a lack of HEA phase diagrams limit the availability of thermodynamic data, some thermodynamic properties, such as atomic size, melting point, mixing entropy, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration, can be used as criteria to predict the phase formation in the HEA system. According to the empirical rules, BCC solid solutions were generally formed in HEA systems under the following certain conditions. (1) The electron concentration (VEC) was lower than 6.87 [ [26] ]; (2) a new parameter combining effects of entropy and enthalpy (Ω) was proposed to be more than 1 and atomic size differences (δ) was less than 6.6% [ [27] ]. δ, Ω, and VEC are calculated to be 5.4, 2.92 and 4.80 respectively, so BCC solid solution could be anticipated, which tallied well with the research results produced by H. Chen et al. [ [13] ]. Guo et al. [ [28] ] further proposed that all ductile alloys have a VEC ≤ 4.4, while all brittle alloys have a VEC ≥ 4.6. Therefore, the NbMoCrTiAl RHEA should be without ductility and it is indeed a type of brittle RHEA.

3.1. Feedstock and SPS Sample Characterisation

The microstructure and morphology of the atomised powder were investigated in cross-sections. The SEM image is shown in Figure 1 a. The single particles exhibit a predominantly spherical shape. A dendritic structure with distinct BSE contrast can be observed, indicating a deviating chemical composition. Due to the high cooling rates during the atomisation process and hence fast solidification, a microstructure with a finer distribution of the phases occurs in comparison to arc-melted samples of the same alloy [ [11] ].
